title: MEP-CMAP Analyser

creators.name: Andrushko, Justin W.
creators.affiliation: School of Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, UK

description:
MEP-CMAP Analyser is a BIDS-compliant, open-source, cross-platform desktop application for processing, quantifying and group-analysing transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and electromyography (EMG) neurophysiology recordings. It is built for researchers who need reproducible, auditable waveform analysis without writing custom scripts for every study.

The tool is not limited to a single measure or paradigm. It handles motor evoked potentials (MEPs), compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs), cortical silent periods (cSPs), M-wave recruitment curves, paired-pulse protocols such as short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) and intracortical facilitation (ICF), and any other time-locked EMG response measurable by peak-to-peak amplitude, onset latency or area under the curve. It operates on continuous recordings, pre-epoched trial stacks, and EMG bursts recorded without stimulation.

Capabilities

  • Direct import of Spike2, LabChart, EDF/BDF, AcqKnowledge and generic delimited text files, with a guided one-time wizard for arbitrary tabular layouts
  • Configurable filtering, including band-pass, notch and harmonic suppression, with live preview
  • Automated detection of response onset, offset and duration, peak-to-peak amplitude, root-mean-square amplitude, area under the curve and cortical silent period duration, each overridable per trial
  • Seven onset detection methods spanning derivative, amplitude-threshold, energy-operator and change-point approaches, with an optional consensus across them and per-trial reporting of how far they disagree
  • Automated outlier screening with an interactive review step, so exclusion decisions are explicit, persistent and recorded in the output
  • An interactive per-trial data inspector for marker adjustment, annotation and exclusion
  • Mmax normalisation with robust plateau detection across full recruitment curves, supramaximal clusters or a single M-wave
  • Compensation of evoked-potential magnitude for pre-stimulus spinal motoneurone excitability by quantile regression, following the method of Carson (2026, Journal of Physiology 604.14, 5731-5757), verified against the author's published reference implementation
  • Paired-pulse ratio computation with multiple reference assignments per file
  • Trial-level and summary CSV output, a group-level file formatted for linear mixed-effects modelling, per-trial waveform bundles, and BIDS-style derivatives with provenance

Changes in version 1.3.3

  • Correction: onset detection was constrained by the amplitude measurement window. The window within which onset was sought was taken from the peak-to-peak window, which is a single setting for the whole recording, while the physiological latency profile is defined per stimulus type. A stimulus type whose profile began earlier than the amplitude window start therefore had its onsets pinned to the edge of that window. Measured on a deltoid-like case with a true onset of 8.9 milliseconds, a profile of 8 to 16 milliseconds and the default 10 to 50 millisecond window, every trial returned exactly 10.00 milliseconds with a between-trial standard deviation of zero. The failure is more damaging than a detector that returns nothing, because implausibly consistent latencies read as unusually clean data. The search window is now derived from the latency profile, widened by the amplitude window and floored at the artefact blanking period, and the log reports whenever the onsets of a condition collapse onto a search bound.
  • Correction: the interactive inspector detected onsets differently from the analysis. The inspector carried its own copy of the detector dispatch. That copy knew only four methods, so selecting a newer one fell through to the peak-fraction method without comment, and it forwarded neither the minimum amplitude gate nor the peak fraction nor the slope threshold, so those reverted to the detectors' own defaults. A re-detection performed while reviewing a trial could therefore use a different algorithm, and different settings, from the analysis that produced the value it replaced. Both paths now call one implementation, and the equivalence is asserted by test across every registered method.
  • New measures: MEP offset and duration. The end of the evoked response is reported as MEP_Offset(ms) and the interval from onset as MEP_Duration(ms). A single precedence rule is applied and MEP_Offset_Source records which branch produced the value: a manual marker takes precedence; otherwise, where a cortical silent period is enabled and detected, its start is the end of the response and is reported as such, because the two are the same physical event; otherwise the return of the envelope to baseline is detected. The return criterion is the larger of a baseline-derived level and a fraction of the response's own peak, because an absolute threshold tied to a quiet resting baseline fails more often the larger and cleaner the response: real electromyography does not settle to a resting-quiet level within tens of milliseconds of a large evoked potential. Detecting the offset also gives area under the curve a defined endpoint in resting-state recordings, where there is no silent period to close the integration window and the endpoint previously had to be placed by hand.
  • New onset detection methods. Four additions bring the total to seven. A root-mean-square envelope method thresholds a smoothed envelope at a multiple of the baseline standard deviation, with the minimum duration calibrated against the chance distribution of above-threshold run lengths rather than fixed by hand, and with the coarse crossing refined on a much shorter window so that the reported latency is largely independent of the smoothing width. A cumulative sum method reports the point at which the mean of the signal changed rather than the point at which it crossed a level, which is the quantity an onset latency is intended to measure. Teager-Kaiser energy preconditioning is available on both, amplifying components that are simultaneously large and fast-changing. A consensus method reports the median across a configurable set of the others.
  • New option: amplitude window anchored per stimulus type. The amplitude window is one setting for the whole recording, so a file containing both M-waves and motor evoked potentials cannot be measured correctly by a single window. On a recording of that kind the M-wave conditions had the first six milliseconds of every response excluded from the measurement, understating their amplitude by approximately twenty percent, because an M-wave's entire biphasic deflection lasts only five to fifteen milliseconds. When enabled, each stimulus type receives a window placed on its own median detected onset. Anchoring is per stimulus type and not per trial, so that onset-detection error does not propagate into the primary amplitude measure and every trial in a condition is measured over a common window; the configured window end still applies as a ceiling. Off by default.
  • New outputs: comparison of the onset detection methods. With per-trial method comparison enabled, every consensus member runs on every trial irrespective of which method is selected, and the spread between them is reported as Onset_Disagreement(ms), which identifies the trials warranting manual review. The individual latencies are written to a long-format table and a per-method summary, and to figures showing where each method's onset falls on the condition's own waveform, the distribution of latency by method, the distribution of disagreement, and a Bland-Altman comparison of each method against a leave-one-out consensus. The reference excludes the method under test because comparing a method with a composite that contains it is a part-whole comparison, which draws the bias toward zero and narrows the limits of agreement; on a real recording this understated the limits by approximately a quarter. Agreement between methods is not accuracy, and the outputs say so: detectors sharing an assumption may be wrong together.
  • Superseded defaults now reach existing installations. The preferences dialogue writes every field on the tab, so a value the analyst never deliberately chose was stored and thereafter took precedence over any later revision of that default. Detection settings are now version-stamped and migrated when the preferences file is read, but only where the stored value is still the default it superseded, so a deliberate choice is never overwritten. A button restores the shipped detection defaults outright.
  • The amplitude window fields are relabelled and now state that they do not constrain onset detection, which is governed by each stimulus type's latency profile. The minimum amplitude gate, peak fraction and slope threshold are applied consistently by the analysis and by the inspector. Detection defaults are defined in one place, with a test that fails if the pipeline, the preferences or the interface drift apart from it.

Note on reproducibility: recordings should be reprocessed if onset latency or area under the curve was used. The onset correction described above changes the reported latency for any stimulus type whose physiological latency profile began earlier than the amplitude window start; in affected files those latencies were the edge of the search window rather than a measurement, and are recognisable by being identical across trials. Area under the curve gains a defined endpoint in resting-state recordings, where it was previously either absent or bounded by a manually placed marker. Peak-to-peak amplitude, root-mean-square amplitude, the cortical silent period measures, the normalised and excitability-compensated amplitudes and the stored waveforms are unaffected by these items, so an analysis resting only on those is unchanged. Recordings analysed with version 1.3.1 or earlier should additionally be reprocessed for the trial-level column alignment corrected in version 1.3.2, and those analysed with the excitability compensation in version 1.2.5 or earlier for the reason noted at version 1.2.8.
